items.title: Load the NW-BRaVE CP12 MD dataset (Activity 4) into the lambda lakehouse tenant
items.body:
## Goal

Load the NW-BRaVE cyanophage CP12 molecular dynamics release into the `lambda` tenant of the BER Data Lakehouse, as a new database `lambda.nwbrave_cp12`. This is the first Activity 4 use-case dataset, and the first step on the Year 1 Task 4 commitment to load Activity 4 metadata into BRIDGE (see #139).

The metadata goes into tables. The bytes stay where they were published: every file row carries a URI, a size and a checksum.

## Source data

| What | Identifier |
|---|---|
| Analysis package: trajectories, scripts and processed tables (16 files, 3.04 GB, CC-BY-4.0) | Zenodo [10.5281/zenodo.21536143](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21536143) |
| Preprint | bioRxiv [10.64898/2026.09.10.750766](https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.10.750766) |
| EMSL project 61054, MED4 | [10.25582/data.2026-08.3856177/3407882](https://doi.org/10.25582/data.2026-08.3856177/3407882) |
| EMSL project 61054, MED4 with phage P-HM2 | [10.25582/data.2026-08.3853205/3407881](https://doi.org/10.25582/data.2026-08.3853205/3407881) |
| Proteomics | MassIVE MSV000102848 |

The release covers GROMACS 2025.0 MD of the *Prochlorococcus* MED4 GAP2·CP12·PRK dark complex (GAP2×8, PRK×4, CP12×4, NAD×8). There are two variants: host CP12, and cyanophage P-HM2 CP12 (UniProt E3ST77) in place of the host CP12. Each was run reduced (0000) and oxidized (0003), with 3 × 100 ns replicates per state, giving 12 `.xtc` files. A 1,012-system cysteine PTM set per variant was also run with ptmpsi; its trajectories were not released.

## Inputs (already built, in PR #140)

Merge #140 first, or work from its branch `cmungall/nwbrave-cp12-md`.


- `tests/data/valid/Dataset-nwbrave-cp12.yaml`: the lambda-ber-schema `Dataset` record, 319 rows over 24 slots. Passes `linkml-validate`, `linkml-run-examples` and the Pydantic loader.
- `tests/data/rocrate/valid/nwbrave-cp12-md.json`: a LAMBDA Core 0.3.4 detached RO-Crate with 76 entities and a sha256 on every Zenodo file, including `trajectories.zip` (its md5 was checked against Zenodo's). It passes `lambda-ber-schema rocrate validate`. The root `@id` is the intended bronze location, `s3a://cdm-lake/tenant-general-warehouse/lambda/datasets/nwbrave_cp12/`, and the LAMBDA record is a part at `nwbrave_cp12_lambda_ber.yaml` in the same directory. The crate pins that record's sha256, so upload the record byte for byte.
- Preview of the intended result: tables, example queries, crate and gaps. https://claude.ai/artifact/P8sGsDb9V8veK1zxRaH9GF (private; ask @cmungall for access)

## What to do

1. **Get #140 and #139 items 1 and 2 merged first**, or do the work on top of them. Today's `ENTITY_SLOTS` drops 10 of this dataset's 24 tables, 97 rows in all: `proteins`, `small_molecules`, `sample_components`, `sample_component_interactions`, `sample_protein_associations`, `persons`, `organizations` and three person/organization association tables.
2. **Give `scripts/ingest_to_lakehouse.py` a way to load a finished Dataset record.** Today it accepts only `sasbdb`, `simplescattering` and `ssrl-mx` (`SUPPORTED_SOURCES`, line 34; rejected at line 519) and expects a loader to dump one YAML file per entry. Add an option that takes a directory of finished Dataset YAMLs plus a dataset name, and skips the dump step. With `--skip-dump --dump-dir` that may be as small as relaxing the source check for a named dataset. Add a pytest test that converts `Dataset-nwbrave-cp12.yaml` and checks that all 24 slots produce Parquet.
3. **Upload to bronze** under `s3a://cdm-lake/tenant-general-warehouse/lambda/datasets/nwbrave_cp12/`:
   - one Parquet file per slot, plus `nwbrave_cp12_ingest_config.json`, as the script writes them;
   - `ro-crate-metadata.json`, a copy of `tests/data/rocrate/valid/nwbrave-cp12-md.json`;
   - `nwbrave_cp12_lambda_ber.yaml`, a byte-identical copy of `tests/data/valid/Dataset-nwbrave-cp12.yaml`.
   The script does not upload the last two today. Upload them by hand, or extend the script.
4. **Ingest to silver** as `lambda.nwbrave_cp12` (`data_files` becomes `dataset_files` as usual). Check the new table names against Iceberg reserved names, as #139 notes.
5. **Check the result and report it here.** Post row counts per table; they should match the table below. Also post the output of the three queries in the next section, run against silver.

### Expected row counts

| Table | Rows | | Table | Rows |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| studies | 1 | | study_sample_associations | 8 |
| persons | 10 | | study_experiment_associations | 6 |
| organizations | 6 | | study_workflow_associations | 28 |
| instruments | 2 | | study_person_associations | 10 |
| proteins | 4 | | study_organization_associations | 4 |
| small_molecules | 1 | | person_organization_associations | 10 |
| samples | 8 | | experiment_sample_associations | 6 |
| sample_components | 16 | | experiment_instrument_associations | 6 |
| experiment_runs | 6 | | sample_protein_associations | 24 |
| workflow_runs | 28 | | sample_component_interactions | 12 |
| dataset_files | 38 | | workflow_experiment_associations | 44 |
| | | | workflow_input_associations | 4 |
| | | | workflow_output_associations | 28 |

### Smoke-test queries

```sql
-- 1. What each simulated complex contains: 12 rows; the HM2 rows show CP12 from NCBITaxon:445696
select s.sample_code, p.gene_name, p.organism, spa.copy_number, spa.modifications
from sample_protein_associations spa
join samples s  on s.id = spa.sample_id
join proteins p on p.id = spa.protein_id
where s.sample_code like '%-000_'
order by s.sample_code, p.gene_name;

-- 2. Simulation time per campaign: 300 ns for each of the four reference conditions
select e.experiment_code, count(distinct w.id) as production_runs
from experiment_runs e
join workflow_experiment_associations we on we.experiment_id = e.id
join workflow_runs w on w.id = we.workflow_id and w.workflow_type = 'md_production'
group by 1 order by 1;

-- 3. Join to the rest of BERDL: the three UniProt-identified proteins
select id, gene_name, organism from proteins where id like 'uniprot:%';
```

Query 3 is the point of the exercise: `uniprot:Q7TUI0` (GAP2), `uniprot:Q7V1S0` (PRK) and `uniprot:E3ST77` (phage CP12) should join to the genome and pangenome collections in BERDL. MED4 CP12 (locus PMM0220) has no UniProtKB entry and is `lambda:protein-med4-cp12-PMM0220`; its UniParc id is UPI0000D9F8C8.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `lambda.nwbrave_cp12` exists in silver with all 24 tables and the row counts above.
- [ ] Bronze holds the Parquet files, the ingest config, `ro-crate-metadata.json` and `nwbrave_cp12_lambda_ber.yaml`, and the record's sha256 matches the one in the crate.
- [ ] The ingest script can load a finished Dataset record, with a pytest test that needs no lakehouse access.
- [ ] `make test` and `pytest` pass.
- [ ] Row counts and the output of the three queries are posted here.
- [ ] #95 is updated to show the first Activity 4 deposit.

## Out of scope / known limits

- **Do not download or upload the trajectories.** `trajectories.zip` is 2.98 GB and stays on Zenodo; `dataset_files.storage_uri` points at it.
- **MD results are in description text, not columns.** Buried surface area, MM/GBSA and contact occupancy have no schema slots. These are schema issues; don't work around them in the ingest.
- **One row stands for 1,012 systems.** Each PTM set is a single Sample and a single production run.
- **Some links are opaque.** The EMSL DataCite records have no description, and MassIVE MSV000102848 returns 404 from PROXI. The crate records them as remote parts and declares what is missing.
- **Nested objects are JSON strings.** Fields such as `md_simulation_params` are stored as JSON strings in Parquet, as for the other sources.

## Access needed

Steps 3 to 5 need BERDL MinIO and Spark/Polaris credentials for the `lambda` tenant (`berdl_notebook_utils`, `data_lakehouse_ingest`). Steps 1 and 2 need none.

items.title: Lakehouse ingest: write molecular entity tables, derive slots from the schema, de-duplicate shared entities
items.body:
## Problem

The `lambda` tenant in the BER lakehouse was loaded by `scripts/ingest_to_lakehouse.py` in May–June 2026. The schema has gained several entity tables since then, and the script has not kept up. The live tenant (comparison made against schema commit `6f146a5`) has these gaps:

| Database | Experiment runs | Dataset files | Tables |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lambda.sasbdb` | 5,358 | 26,015 | 10 |
| `lambda.simplescattering` | 86 | 386 | 9 |
| `lambda.ssrl_mx` | 4 | 4 | 13 |

### 1. Slots the script never writes

`ENTITY_SLOTS` is a hard-coded tuple, last changed 6 June. These multivalued `Dataset` slots in the current schema are missing from it:

- `proteins`, `nucleic_acids`, `small_molecules`
- `sample_components`, `sample_component_interactions`
- `sample_protein_associations`, `sample_nucleic_acid_associations`
- `persons`, `organizations` and their associations: `study_person_associations`, `experiment_person_associations`, `workflow_person_associations`, `study_organization_associations`, `person_organization_associations`

All five current loaders (PDB, SASBDB, SimpleScattering, SSRL MX, ANL) already emit `proteins`. The script just drops them. This is the main gap: the protein table is where the UniProt CURIEs live, and without it the structural data cannot join to genomes or anything else in BERDL. Today `samples` only has `protein_name`, plus `database_cross_references` in two databases.

### 2. Duplicated shared entities

Each per-entry YAML carries its own copy of its instrument, and `convert_yamls_to_parquet` appends rows without de-duplicating. `sasbdb.instruments` has 5,358 rows for 113 distinct instrument codes; `simplescattering.instruments` has 86 rows for 1. The same will happen to `proteins`, `nucleic_acids` and `small_molecules` once they are written, since one UniProt entry appears in many SASBDB entries.

### 3. Stale load

The tenant reflects the loaders and schema of mid-2026. Since then: protein, nucleic acid and small-molecule tables (#120, #124), UniProt CURIEs, instrument subclasses (#129) and more.

## Proposed changes

1. **Derive the slot list from the schema** instead of hard-coding it. Use the multivalued, class-ranged slots of `Dataset` via `SchemaView.class_induced_slots("Dataset")`, or the pydantic `Dataset` model's list fields, so the script cannot go stale again. Keep `SLOT_TO_SILVER_NAME` (`data_files` → `dataset_files`).
2. **De-duplicate shared entity tables** (`instruments`, `proteins`, `nucleic_acids`, `small_molecules`, `persons`, `organizations`) by `id`, with `instrument_code` as a fallback for instruments.
   - Check that rows sharing an `id` are identical, and log any conflicts rather than silently keeping the first.
   - Entry-level tables keep `source_entry_id`. Shared tables need a way back to their entries: the existing association tables cover samples to proteins and nucleic acids. Add a `source_entry_ids` list column only if something is still missing.
3. **Re-dump and re-ingest** SASBDB, SimpleScattering and SSRL MX with the current loaders and schema.
   - Hold PDB until its overlap with `kescience.pdb` is settled.
   - Note #101: the SASBDB and SimpleScattering loaders treat every entry as SAXS, so SANS entries in SASBDB are mislabelled until that is fixed.
4. **Report join-key coverage** after re-ingest:
   - the fraction of samples with a linked protein carrying a UniProt CURIE;
   - how many `database_cross_references` resolve to UniProt or to `kescience.pdb`.
5. **Tests.** Add pytest tests for slot derivation (every multivalued class-ranged `Dataset` slot is covered) and for de-duplication (shared rows collapse; conflicting rows are reported), using a few YAMLs from `tests/data/valid/`. No live lakehouse calls in CI.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ENTITY_SLOTS` is derived from the schema; a test fails if a new multivalued `Dataset` slot is not ingested.
- [ ] `instruments`, `proteins`, `nucleic_acids` and `small_molecules` have one row per `id` in each database.
- [ ] `lambda.sasbdb`, `lambda.simplescattering` and `lambda.ssrl_mx` are re-ingested from current loaders and include `proteins` and `sample_protein_associations`.
- [ ] The join-key coverage report is posted as a comment on this issue.
- [ ] `make test` and `pytest` pass.

## Context

This also starts the Year 1 Task 4 commitment, due Q1 FY2027: load metadata for Activity 4's use-case datasets into BRIDGE. Those datasets have not been delivered yet. Related: #95 (ETL tracking per site), #101, #137 (validating against the full schema), PR #103 and PR #107 (the original ingest work).

items.title: Infra: move the ETL schemas (62 GB of 133 GB) off the primary, and size the primary to the remaining hot set
items.body:
## Context

Measured on production (11–19 Sep 2026): the primary is a burstable **db.t4g.large** (2 vCPU, 8 GB, $122/month) sitting at **0 CPU credit balance all week**, with 15 h/week above 70% CPU, and the slow requests come in **incidents**, not spread evenly — a tiny org (Udgam, ~1.1 k subjects) suffered 520–700 s requests as collateral damage while another org ran 22 concurrent assignment searches. The database was saturated; whose query it was mattered less than that it was running.

The code fixes (#1067, #1068, #1069, avniproject/avni-client#2096, avniproject/avni-client#2099, #1057) remove an estimated **40–50% of primary database time**, rising to ~55% with #1057. Two infrastructure items remain, and they should be decided **after** those land, because the required size depends on the hot set that is left.

## 1. Move the ETL schemas off the primary

The primary holds **133 GB, of which the ETL schemas are 62 GB**. They compete with the transactional hot set for the same shared buffers and the same IOPS. Metabase reads the ETL schemas, not the tables the code fixes touch — measured: replica-vs-primary for the same reporting query is within 25% (contention is not the constraint) while cold-vs-warm is **20–60×** (cache residency is). Moving the ETL schemas to their own instance frees cache for the transactional workload and is the main lever for reporting latency.

## 2. Size the instance to the hot set

The saving from the code fixes is **not** a smaller instance — it is **avoiding the upgrade** the current trajectory demands. Options priced (ap-south-1, on-demand): db.t4g.xlarge **$244/mo**, db.m7g.large **$175/mo**, db.r7g.large **$199/mo**, against today's **$122/mo**. Staying on db.t4g.large avoids **$53–122/month**. A non-burstable class also removes the credit-exhaustion cliff, which is the mechanism behind the incident pattern.

## To decide

- [ ] Whether the ETL schemas move to a separate instance, and when.
- [ ] Whether the primary moves to a non-burstable class now or after the code fixes are measured in production.
- [ ] Re-measure CPU credits, ReadIOPS and DiskQueueDepth after each code fix reaches production, so the sizing decision uses post-fix numbers.

**Dropped after measurement:** a dedicated database for outlier orgs (apfodisha) — partitioning plus the index plus the client change handles it inside the shared database (1,005 s in the best 4-user run, with three other orgs syncing). Also dropped: per-tenant read replicas (operationally heavy, read-only benefit) and ETL tables for search (staleness).

Evidence: `finalreco.md` §"Cost" and recommendations 9–10.

---
Evidence and full write-up: [finalreco.md](https://github.com/avniproject/avni-product-ops/blob/main/analysis/sync-db-performance-sept-2026/finalreco.md) (conclusions) and [reco.md](https://github.com/avniproject/avni-product-ops/blob/main/analysis/sync-db-performance-sept-2026/reco.md) (raw work log) in avni-product-ops. Code: branch [`performancefixes`](https://github.com/avniproject/avni-server/tree/performancefixes). Epic: avniproject/avni-product#1904.

# [Sprint 4 / Wave 4A] Retire Fake Bookkeeping Entities (`claim:*`, `wit:*`, `file:*`, `src:*`, `model:*` Prefix Strings)

## 1. Context & Architectural Law
Implement together with `#1730` and `#1731`:
- Delete `ConsensusKeys.cs` prefix-string hashing (`"claim:"`, `"wit:"`, `"file:"`, `"src:"`, `"model:"`).
- A claim's ID is the Merkle composition ID of its strand vertices; a file's ID is `[metadata, content]`; a witness's ID is its source trunk `[source_record, file_trunks...]`.

## 2. Strict File Ownership Boundary
- Same unit as `#1730` and `#1731`.

## 3. Automated Grading Rubric
- `git grep -nE '"(claim|wit|file|src|model):"' app/ engine/` returns `0` matches.


### Current implementation ownership
This unit owns the actual-arity claim identity boundary in `app/Laplace.Core/Core/ConsensusKeys.cs`, `app/Laplace.Core.Tests/Core/ConsensusKeysParityTests.cs`, `extension/laplace_substrate/src/fold_route.c`, `extension/laplace_substrate/sql/schema/tables/consensus_id.sql.in`, and the corresponding extension regression SQL/expected output. A missing object is absent from the composition, never a zero-filled synthetic vertex. It also owns the existing source/file identity and bootstrap adapters under `app/Laplace.Substrate/Abstractions/` and their tests, together with the native recipe/schema convergence units #1881/#1717/#1885/#1723 for final source-trunk witness registration. Prefix grep alone is not completion.

The Windows extension acceptance build also owns `extension/CMakeLists.txt` to consume the real Native static-library dependency graph introduced by #1731/#1711 (no `_deps/blake3` assumption or omitted ICU/Native text archives).

items.title: MVP: Flat monorepo + working backend/frontend/docs/data + central schema
items.body:
## Goal
Ship a **hackathon-honest MVP** of Klima with a **flat** monorepo (complYaigent-style) and working surfaces for **backend, frontend, docs, and data**, plus a **central schema** shared across packages.

## Target layout
```text
klima/
├── mobile/      # Flutter (keep)
├── backend/     # FastAPI (was web/api)
├── frontend/    # Next LGU dashboard (was web/dashboard)
├── docs/        # VitePress (was web/docs)
├── data/        # ETL + DuckDB assets (canonical pipeline home)
└── schema/      # central contracts (Pydantic / OpenAPI / JSON Schema)
```

Reference flat layout: https://github.com/liitkud/complyaigent (`backend/`, `frontend/`, `docs/`).

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Layout is flat (no `web/` nesting)
- [ ] `backend` boots; health + mobile contract endpoints work
- [ ] `frontend` talks to live backend (not mock-only stub page)
- [ ] `docs` site builds with getting-started + API overview
- [ ] `data` owns ETL; bronze ingest runnable via documented command
- [ ] `schema/` is single source of truth for hazard/report/safezone/community models
- [ ] README + STATUS match reality
- [ ] Each workstream has a handoff under `docs/handoffs/`

## Non-goals (post-MVP)
- Production Auth0/Keycloak multi-tenant RBAC
- Full silver/gold medallion orchestration + schedulers
- Channel bots (Messenger/Telegram/Viber)
- Perfect offline sync on mobile

## Children
- #3 Flatten
- #4 Central schema
- #5 Backend
- #6 Frontend
- #7 Docs
- #8 Data

**Branch:** `docs/mvp-handoffs` — [mvp plan](https://github.com/Signal-No-5/klima/blob/docs/mvp-handoffs/docs/mvp/README.md)

items.title: Docs: Maintenance and Support Guide for BIAR
items.body:
# Maintenance and Support Guide for BIAR

**Repository:** `tazama-lf/biar`  
**Audience:** Developers and maintainers contributing code to the BIAR platform

---

> **Note to authors:** The headings and descriptors in this outline are suggestions. They are not exhaustive — add, remove, or reorganise sections to reflect what the BIAR platform actually requires. The intent is to prompt coverage, not to prescribe structure.

---

## 1. Introduction

Purpose and scope of this guide; intended audience; how this guide relates to other BIAR documentation ([BIAR README](https://github.com/tazama-lf/biar/blob/dev/README.md), requirements specification, [NiFi Deployment Guide](https://github.com/tazama-lf/docs/blob/dev/Technical/Deployment-Guides/Nifi-Deployment-Guide.md)).

---

## 2. Architecture Overview

> *The README documents the component list, ports, and technology stack. Extend this with the runtime data flow diagram showing how NiFi, Ozone, the Automation Orchestrator, Hudi, and JupyterHub interact end-to-end, and how the medallion layers (Bronze / Silver / Gold / Views) map to warehouse paths.*

---

## 3. Development Environment Setup

> *The README covers prerequisites and `docker compose up -d`. Extend this with the full environment variable configuration required before first run, how to verify all services are healthy after startup, and any local mock or stub options for development without a live PostgreSQL connection.*

---

## 4. Repository Structure

A map of the directory layout explaining the purpose of each folder and the key files a contributor will need to edit for common tasks (adding an ETL, modifying a NiFi flow, updating a notebook).

---

## 5. The ETL Pipeline — How It Works

End-to-end walkthrough of a single record from PostgreSQL to Gold layer, covering NiFi extraction, Ozone storage, the `/checksubmit` trigger, `FullETLOrchestrator` dispatch, the `BaseETL` Bronze/Silver/Gold execution model, and the Views trigger.

### 5.1 `FullETLOrchestrator` and `_ETL_REGISTRY`

### 5.2 `BaseETL` — The ETL Contract

### 5.3 Standard Hudi Write Settings

> *The canonical record of Hudi write settings is the `BaseETL` class itself. Add docstrings to the relevant constants and methods in `BaseETL` if not yet present, then refer the reader to the class rather than maintaining a separate list here.*

### 5.4 Views Layer and `ViewsOrchestrator`

---

## 6. Adding or Modifying an ETL Pipeline

Step-by-step guide for implementing a new domain ETL class, registering it, and following the layer conventions.

### 6.1 Creating a New ETL Class (BaseETL subclass)

### 6.2 Bronze Layer Conventions

> *The mandatory bookkeeping columns, record hash approach, and type casting rules should be documented as docstrings on `BaseETL.build_bronze()` — add them if not yet present. Refer the reader to that docstring here; do not duplicate the specification in this guide.*

### 6.3 Silver Layer Conventions

> *Column renaming, timestamp parsing, JSON parsing, deduplication, and DQ split conventions should be documented as docstrings on `BaseETL.build_silver()` — add them if not yet present. Refer the reader to that docstring here.*

### 6.4 Gold Layer Conventions

> *Scalar-only column requirements, surrogate key derivation, partitioning, and payload class choices should be documented as docstrings on `BaseETL.build_gold()` — add them if not yet present. Refer the reader to that docstring here.*

### 6.5 Adding a DQ / DLQ Path

Covers the DQ/DLQ pattern, including example rules, reason codes, and the `silver/{table}_dlq` path convention; `AlertsETL` is the reference implementation.

---

## 7. NiFi Flow Management

> *The README notes NiFi uses `tazama.xml` and `init.sh` configures parameter contexts. Extend this with the steps to add a new `QueryDatabaseTableRecord` processor for a new source table, the required `<properties>` values (watermark column, batch size, schedule, record writer), how to add the corresponding `InvokeHTTP` trigger, and how to reload the flow after changes.*

---

## 8. JupyterHub Notebooks — Maintenance

> *The README lists the notebook names. Each notebook is expected to be self-documented (purpose, inputs, assumptions, and known limitations in markdown cells). Extend this with the operational conventions a developer must follow when working with notebooks.*

### 8.1 Connecting to the Lakehouse

Using `WAREHOUSE_ROOT` and the `load_tenant_hudi()` helper to read Hudi tables with tenant filtering. Note: `load_tenant_hudi()` is currently defined inline in each notebook (copy-paste pattern). Consider extracting it to a shared `notebook_utils.py` module with a proper docstring — if extracted, refer the reader to that module here. If it remains inline, the function definition in each notebook's setup cell is the canonical reference.

### 8.2 Metric Calculation Conventions

Covers aggregation approaches, disposition filters, and suggested validation steps when writing or modifying metric calculations.

### 8.3 Adding a New Notebook

> *A `_template.ipynb` committed to the `JupyterHub/notebooks/` directory is the most effective way to enforce notebook structure — create it if it does not yet exist, then refer the reader to it here. If no template is created, document the required structure in this section instead (purpose cell, inputs cell, assumptions and limitations, output description, cleared outputs before commit).*

---

## 9. The Datalakehouse Query API

> *The README describes this as a "query service with thread-safe Spark session management". `lakehouse_query_api.py` already generates an OpenAPI schema via `custom_openapi()`. The recommended approach is to export this as a committed `openapi.json` (or equivalent) and refer the reader to it from this section — the Swagger UI is also available at `/docs` on the running service. If an exported schema is not created, document the available endpoints, the shared Spark session model, and the rule against creating additional `SparkSession` instances in this section as a fallback.*

---

## 10. The Unstructured Document Pipeline

> *The README describes the five-step document processing flow. Extend this with the required environment variables (including encryption key management), file size limits, retry behaviour, and how to add support for a new document type or MIME type exclusion.*

---

## 11. Testing

**TypeScript (unstructured pipeline):** From the `unstructured-pipeline/` directory — `npm test` (run once), `npm run test:watch` (watch mode), `npm run test:coverage` (with coverage report). These commands are also in `unstructured-pipeline/README.md`.

**Python ETL tests:** No pytest suite currently exists for the automation orchestrator. Document how to run the suite here once it is created. Include suggested approaches for writing tests for a new `BaseETL` subclass — for example, providing a mock `SparkSession` and asserting on the Bronze / Silver / Gold Hudi table write calls.

items.title: SPEC: Claims Analyst Agent

labels.description: Fully specified, ready for an AFK agent

items.body:
# SPEC: Claims Analyst Agent

Status: `ready-for-agent`

## Problem Statement

Healthcare claims auditors manually sift through massive datasets (CMS SynPUF) looking for fraud, waste, and abuse patterns — upcoding, readmission spirals, geographic anomalies. The data is too large and the patterns too subtle for human-only review. Auditors need an AI agent that can autonomously detect anomalous claim signals, form and test hypotheses against a knowledge graph of known fraud patterns, and produce structured, evidence-backed findings they can act on.

## Solution

A multi-stage autonomous claims analyst agent that:

1. **Ingests** CMS SynPUF claims data through an ETL pipeline into SQLite, computing baseline statistics for signal detection
2. **Detects** statistical anomalies (signals) using rule-based heuristics, groups related signals, and enriches them with graph context from a Kuzu knowledge graph
3. **Reasons** about each signal cluster: pulls the relevant subgraph, generates hypotheses from known fraud-pattern edges, spawns focused sub-agents to test each hypothesis against the data, and synthesizes a structured finding card with scored verdicts

The system ships with three seeded fraud scenarios (upcoding, readmission spiral, geographic spike) to validate the full pipeline end-to-end.

## User Stories

1. As an auditor, I want the system to detect when a provider's DRG coding distribution differs significantly from their peers, so that I can investigate potential upcoding.
2. As an auditor, I want the system to detect when a provider's 30-day readmission rate exceeds the baseline, so that I can investigate quality-of-care or fraud issues.
3. As an auditor, I want the system to detect geographic anomalies in service volume, so that I can investigate whether a local outbreak, miscoding, or new facility explains the spike.
4. As an auditor, I want each detected anomaly to be enriched with graph context (peer relationships, DRG hierarchies, regional norms), so that I understand the signal in its full context before the agent reasons about it.
5. As an auditor, I want the agent to autonomously generate multiple hypotheses for each anomaly from a library of known fraud and abuse patterns, so that no plausible explanation is missed.
6. As an auditor, I want each hypothesis to be tested by a focused sub-agent that receives only the data relevant to that question, so that each test is unbiased and efficient.
7. As an auditor, I want the agent to produce a structured finding card per signal cluster that includes the original signal, the hypotheses tested, each sub-agent's scored verdict, and a synthesized summary, so that I can review and act on the findings.
8. As an auditor, I want the finding card to include an evidence path (which data was queried, which graph edges were traversed, which hypotheses were rejected and why), so that the reasoning is auditable.
9. As a developer, I want the shared types, DRG codes, region maps, and signal schemas in a single shared package, so that all other packages stay in sync.
10. As a developer, I want the ETL pipeline to be reproducible from seed CSV files, so that I can rebuild the database deterministically for testing.
11. As a developer, I want the knowledge graph to encode a KPI hierarchy (which metrics influence which) and hypothesis edges (which fraud patterns map to which testable queries), so that the agent's reasoning is grounded in domain knowledge rather than free-form text.
12. As a developer, I want the agent architecture to be protocol-driven (signal → graph enrichment → hypothesis generation → sub-agent testing → synthesis), so that each stage is independently testable and the flow is predictable.
13. As an auditor, I want to view findings in a dashboard with a signal feed, investigation panels, and finding cards, so that I can triage alerts by severity and drill into details.
14. As an auditor, I want the dashboard to support conversational interaction with the agent (ask follow-up questions about a finding), so that I can explore findings interactively.
15. As a developer, I want the three seeded scenarios to serve as integration tests for the full pipeline, so that I can validate end-to-end correctness before adding new scenarios.

## Implementation Decisions

### Monorepo structure

The project uses a Turborepo monorepo with five packages:

- **shared**: Types, constants (DRG codes, region mappings), signal schemas, Zod validators
- **data**: ETL from CMS SynPUF CSVs into SQLite via better-sqlite3 + drizzle-orm. Computes baseline statistics (mean, stddev, percentile thresholds) per DRG, provider, and region. Seeds reference data from checked-in CSVs.
- **graph**: Kuzu embedded graph database. Schema defines KPI hierarchy nodes (metric → provider → region → DRG family → DRG) with influence edges, and hypothesis edges mapping fraud patterns to testable Cypher queries. Seeded from SQLite after ETL.
- **agents**: Multi-stage pipeline: (1) statistical rule engine detects anomalous signals from SQLite baselines, (2) heuristic grouper clusters related signals, (3) graph enricher attaches Kuzu subgraph context, (4) reasoning agent pulls subgraph, generates hypotheses from hypothesis edges, spawns sub-agents, synthesizes finding card. Built on Vercel AI SDK with OpenAI-compatible model.
- **dashboard**: Next.js App Router + shadcn/ui + AI Elements. Signal feed, investigation panel, finding cards. Conversational chat interface for follow-up queries against findings.

### Data layer decisions

- SQLite (better-sqlite3) for synchronous, embedded access — no server process needed
- drizzle-orm for schema definitions and migrations via drizzle-kit
- Seed CSVs stored in `packages/data/seeds/` — small enough for git (no binary blobs)
- Baseline statistics pre-computed at ETL time and stored in SQLite for fast signal rule evaluation
- pond-ts and als-statistics for statistical computations (z-scores, percentiles, distribution comparisons)

### Graph layer decisions

- Kuzu 0.11.3 embedded — no server, runs in-process
- Graph schema: nodes for Provider, DRG, Region, Claim, Patient, Metric. Edges for SUBMITTED_BY, BELONGS_TO, INFLUENCES, HYPOTHESIZES
- KPI hierarchy edges (INFLUENCES) map metric-to-metric relationships: e.g. DRG coding distribution INFLUENCES average reimbursement
- Hypothesis edges (HYPOTHESIZES) map fraud patterns to testable questions: e.g. "upcoding pattern" → "Is patient mix comparable to peers?" → Cypher query
- Graph seeded from SQLite after ETL completes
- Agent reads-only from graph; graph is rebuilt on each ETL run (not mutated by the agent)

### Agent architecture decisions

The agent follows a protocol-driven, deterministic pipeline before reaching the LLM:

1. **Statistical rule engine**: Evaluates z-score thresholds, peer-comparison baselines, and trend detectors. Emits raw signal objects with confidence scores.
2. **Heuristic grouper**: Clusters signals by provider, DRG family, region, and temporal proximity. Avoids flooding the agent with duplicate alerts.
3. **Graph enricher**: For each signal cluster, queries Kuzu for the relevant subgraph (peer providers, DRG hierarchy, influence edges, hypothesis edges). Attaches it as structured context.
4. **Reasoning agent** (single LLM call): Receives enriched signal cluster + subgraph. Generates hypotheses from the subgraph's hypothesis edges, then for each hypothesis, defines a focused question and data context for a sub-agent.
5. **Sub-agents** (parallel LLM calls): Each receives one hypothesis + question + data context. Returns a scored verdict (confidence 0–1 + rationale + evidence queries run).
6. **Synthesizer** (single LLM call): Collates sub-agent verdicts into a structured finding card with overall severity, key evidence, and recommendation.

The agent never free-forms its hypotheses — they must originate from hypothesis edges in the graph. This keeps reasoning grounded and testable.

### Schema

The finding card output schema (Zod-validated):

```typescript
const FindingCardSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  signalClusterId: z.string(),
  severity: z.enum(["low", "medium", "high", "critical"]),
  title: z.string(),
  summary: z.string(),
  hypotheses: z.array(z.object({
    id: z.string(),
    pattern: z.string(),
    question: z.string(),
    verdict: z.object({
      score: z.number().min(0).max(1),
      rationale: z.string(),
      evidenceQueries: z.array(z.string()),
    }),
  })),
  recommendation: z.string(),
  evidencePath: z.object({
    signals: z.array(z.string()),
    graphEdgesTraversed: z.array(z.string()),
    dataQueriesRun: z.array(z.string()),
  }),
});
```

### Statistical rules

For the three seeded scenarios:

- **Upcoding**: Compare provider's DRG distribution against peer group (same region, same specialty). Flag DRGs where z-score > 2.0 for high-cost codes or z-score < -2.0 for low-cost codes. Control for patient-mix confounding.
- **Readmission spiral**: Compute 30-day readmission rate per provider. Flag providers > 2 stddev above regional mean. Control for patient acuity (comorbidity count, age).
- **Geographic spike**: Compute weekly ER visit volume per region. Flag regions with > 3 stddev week-over-week change. Control for seasonality and population.

### Dashboard decisions

- Next.js App Router with RSC for data loading
- shadcn/ui component library (Tailwind)
- AI Elements for conversational interface: Conversation, Message, Shimmer, Panel
- Finding cards rendered as expandable panels with hypothesis drill-down
- Signal feed sorted by severity, filterable by scenario type

## Testing Decisions

### What makes a good test

- Test external behavior, not implementation details — assert on output shapes and values, not internal function calls
- Each test should set up known input, run the system under test, and assert observable output
- Prefer integration tests over unit tests where a seam naturally exists
- The three seeded scenarios serve as the primary acceptance tests

### Seams

Tests are organized at three seams, highest to lowest:

**Seam 1 — Agent protocol boundary (primary).** The reasoning agent receives a pre-built subgraph + signal context and produces finding cards. This is tested by:
- Creating test fixtures: pre-built subgraphs for each seeded scenario (upcoding, readmission, geographic)
- Feeding fixtures to the reasoning agent
- Asserting finding cards have correct shape (Zod validation), plausible hypotheses (drawn from the fixture's hypothesis edges), and non-trivial verdicts (scores ≠ 0, rationales reference the data)
- Individual sub-agents can mock or pass through a deterministic model for snapshot testing

**Seam 2 — Signal pipeline.** The statistical rules + grouper + enricher are tested by:
- Creating curated SQLite test databases with known anomalies injected
- Running the signal pipeline
- Asserting signals are correctly detected (present where injected, absent where not), groups are formed, and graph enrichment attaches the expected edges

**Seam 3 — ETL.** The data pipeline is tested by:
- Running ETL against seed CSVs
- Asserting SQLite tables exist, row counts match expectations, baseline statistics are correctly computed

### Prior art

These patterns match standard data-pipeline testing conventions — fixture-driven integration tests at the highest seam, curated test databases at the mid seam, and data-quality assertions at the lowest seam.

## Out of Scope

- Real-time claims ingestion (batch processing only for initial release)
- HIPAA compliance engineering (the system uses synthetic CMS data)
- Production deployment, CI/CD, auth — covered in a future milestone
- Additional fraud scenarios beyond the three seeded ones
- Model fine-tuning or custom LLM training
- Dashboard authentication and multi-tenant isolation

## Further Notes

- The three seeded scenarios must be the first thing built — they validate the full pipeline and serve as the acceptance test suite
- The shared package should be the first dependency established, since all other packages depend on its types
- Kuzu is embedded and read-only for the agent — no concurrent write concerns
- Stats computations (pond-ts, als-statistics) run at ETL time, not at query time, to keep signal detection fast
- The knowledge graph is the control plane — all agent reasoning flows through it; new fraud patterns are added as graph edges, not as code changes

items.title: Program: Elsa Agents — reusable agents and workflow collaboration
items.body:
[Codex] On behalf of @sfmskywalker.

## Outcome and authority

Deliver **Elsa Agents**: users define reusable Agents, test and publish them, then employ those published versions in native Elsa workflows and Elsa-powered BPMN processes. Agents have explicit inputs and outputs. Conversation continuity is an explicit optional capability; cross-run memory is a separately configured resource.

Owner instruction, 31 October 2026: "make a complete end to end plan, including research spikes, designs, architecture and implementation, then turn that into a Program, then deliver that end to end". The owner selected specialists first, explicit continuity, Microsoft Agent Framework reuse where appropriate, and Foundry-inspired authoring. This authorizes research, design, implementation, risk-based tests, documentation, scoped PRs, review and permitted merges, and resulting-main qualification. Routine decisions and milestone transitions proceed under that authority. Releases, deployments, provider purchases and activation of external publishers require separate authority. Use an already authorized model connection for live qualification; request the specific missing credential/connection if none exists.

## Product promise

Create Copywriter with name, instructions and a model connection; optional typed inputs, output schema, tools, knowledge and continuity settings progressively expose more power. Publish an immutable version. Find Copywriter in the activity picker, bind its inputs and use its output. Run it from native workflows and BPMN. Inspect the same agent run from the playground or the enclosing process. Compose Copywriter and Proofreader into a bounded editorial process with human approval. Later publish a bounded collaboration team as an equally usable activity.

## Scope and default recommendations

- Elsa owns Agent-owned typed definitions over shared revision storage, version identity, authorized connections, authored input/output contracts, run evidence and workflow integration. SDK objects and credentials are not persisted in artifacts.
- Prefer Microsoft Agent Framework for model-facing agent execution, tool integration and explicit session serialization when the pinned .NET spike demonstrates the required semantics. Keep provider SDKs in adapters. Do not invent a parallel general-purpose agent framework.
- Foundry inspires configuration, playground, evaluation, publishing and inspection. Azure hosting is optional; no Foundry account is required to use Elsa Agents.
- Fresh invocation by default. Explicit conversation handles are tenant/actor scoped, version compatible and serialized or conflict rejected. Sharing a conversation and sharing memory are different choices.
- Inputs and outputs use Elsa's existing JSON/schema conventions. Reject invalid results explicitly. Model settings are capability aware; unsupported temperature or schema settings are not silently accepted.
- Published agent versions appear through the existing activity-provider/publishing mechanism. Native and BPMN invoke one execution contract, with exact version references and explicit upgrade behavior.
- Elsa controls the enclosing process. An Agent Framework collaboration, when enabled, controls bounded internal coordination. One owner per checkpoint/retry/effect boundary; no two engines independently retry the same tool effect.
- Permission, connection, secret, tenant, storage, diagnostics, Studio slots/contributions and workflow lifecycle capabilities use current owning-domain contracts. Preserve Weaver's existing assistant semantics and single-active-provider default.
- Tools require declared scope and execution-time authorization. Mutating tools have explicit policy and exact-request approval where required. The model cannot grant authority. Effects remain at least once unless the destination's idempotency contract is proved.
- Retain accepted model decisions and results for recovery. A restart must not silently ask the model to reconsider a committed decision. An ambiguous provider response/effect boundary has an explicit reconciliation outcome.
- Team MVP: participant references, explicit context handoffs, bounded writer/reviewer and parallel-specialist patterns, completion conditions and usage budgets. Pattern configuration precedes any bespoke graph designer. Free-form team graph authoring requires positive research evidence of need and ownership.

## Relationship to active programs

Run beside the active programs, displace none and reactivate no parked backlog. Consume delivered hosting/publication/native/BPMN contracts. Coordinate shared runtime/Studio changes through the owning issue and claims; do not work an already claimed leaf.

- **Unified Execution #2892 / #2912** retains its existing production collaboration, durable decision, approval, budgeting and recovery obligations. The completed #2913 witness is research evidence, not product acceptance. This Program links to and integrates that work; it does not reparent #2912, mark its obligations complete, or reorder that Program's current implementation lane. Specialist catalog/design work can proceed independently. Shared runtime changes wait for the owning leaf or are delivered there through a valid claim.
- **Weaver #3428** owns the assistant that helps users build/manage Studio resources. This Program owns agents participating in user-authored processes. Reuse independently justified contracts; avoid rewiring Weaver or removing its single-active-provider rule to add model selection for specialists.
- **BPMN** retains its semantics/interchange authority. Bind the existing task/activity mechanism rather than creating agent-specific BPMN token semantics.
- **Connections, Secrets, Identity, Expressions, Hosting** retain their domain contracts. Qualify packaged/custom-host composition, not only a source-tree Workbench.

## Merged plan reconciliation — 4 November 2026

Merged PR #3783 (`4043cbfb155106b74f2a3cef7cd9dd811a67b0e1`) introduces Agent-owned typed source over shared Workflow/Agent revision mechanics. [ADR 0094](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/4043cbfb155106b74f2a3cef7cd9dd811a67b0e1/docs/adr/0094-agent-definitions-own-authored-content-and-providers-publish-activities.md) and [shared revision mapping](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/4043cbfb155106b74f2a3cef7cd9dd811a67b0e1/specs/1179-specialist-agents/contracts/revision-management.md) own the architecture. M0–M3 closure remains historical baseline delivery, not proof of the source revision amendment. T064 and the T065/storage-T069 code landed in PR #3794 (`2a2b6578159dea38d75974d49e9cdb478d857853`), with required exact-head CI and the resulting-main push CI passing. Ordinary-host qualification found a source schema-admission defect, corrected by merged #3829 at `c0b61d8731de3266d14928e8b1624a31c386184d`. Required reviewed-head CI passed; actual resulting main passes 13 normal-host checks, all affected local suites and a fresh 51-package durable-recovery profile ([receipt](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/pull/3829#issuecomment-6639132320)). That older descendant run was cancelled after main advanced. Final #3790 resulting-main qualification is now verified on `9daaa3206cdd98dfb5978468ea354d711415352d`: push CI [41896980296](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/actions/runs/41896980296) succeeded, and a fresh rebuild on the same head passed all 13 normal-host HTTP checks ([receipt](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/3790#issuecomment-6640642944)). Direct OpenAI #3777/#3773 also merged and is included in this combined resulting-main qualification. T066 is in progress: its provider-compilation bridge merged in #3792 (`9810757feeca31791caa226148ca29809615d130`), with required reviewed-head CI passing and its code also covered by the successful descendant-main run above. T066 now has local shared coordination and both typed publication adapters under qualification; operation APIs, remaining publication-policy checks, independent review/CI/merge, T067–T071 and full W1–W8 acceptance remain open.

The owner waived pre-GA backward compatibility: clean initialization/recreation/republish replaces legacy import/backfill, compatibility aliases/readers and mixed-schema rollback. Ordinary exact artifact binding, scoped authority and retry/replay guarantees remain within a supported deployment. No database is deleted by this issue update.

## Shared revision delivery sequence

| Order / spec task | Delivery | Gate / owning milestone |
|---|---|---|
| T064 + T065 + storage part of T069 | #3790 — shared working copies/snapshots, real Workflow and Agent adapters, provenance and pin/CAS qualification | Demonstrated common implementation before API freeze; impacts the prior M2 baseline without reopening its historical closure |
| T066 + publication part of T069 | Shared operation/review/reservation/receipt coordination; provider compilation for Agent projections and Workflow publication adapters | One executable-publication authority; both lost-reply recovery paths; elaborate successor after first leaf |
| T067 | Declared pre-GA package/schema break, fresh initialization/recreation/republish | No legacy migration required; host/profile/readiness and reference/reset scope explicit |
| T068 | Agent Studio/API integration with shared revision callbacks and read-only generated activity navigation | M5 source/create/test/publish/use/inspect journeys; no UI-to-model shortcut |
| T069–T070 | Per-slice causal controls, native/BPMN, normal hosts/packages, four-provider storage and actual product qualification | M4/M5/M7 and W1–W8 remain open until observed evidence |
| T071 | Prune replaced engines/compatibility scaffolding, reconcile evidence and final lifecycle | M7; no checked historical receipt silently recertifies the new architecture |

The source-storage leaf #3790 is merged. The concrete next T066 publication scope is recorded in [this parent comment](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/3519#issuecomment-6635364775); keep it on this parent while the repository exceeds its ready-issue cap. Consume the merged compiler bridge #3792; its owner completed that contribution and descendant-main qualification is verified above. Do not duplicate its provider compiler/evaluator work. Keep later slices on these milestone checklists until their inputs are concrete. One active implementation leaf plus review lane remains the limit; preserve existing M5 claims and reviewed runtime/provider contributions.

## Shared execution capability dependencies

| Capability | Owner / current evidence | Agent gate |
|---|---|---|
| Durable native background work, checkpoint/result delivery, restart and cancellation | Program #2892; delivered #2914 and #3056 | M3/M4 use existing native runtime primitives and retain exact journal acceptance versus process application; qualify new consumers rather than copy a scheduler |
| BPMN semantics/hosting and parent continuation | Delivered #2898; ongoing #2907 retains first-class BPMN operational ownership | M4 qualifies Agent binding/runtime-only closure; concrete missing shared capability goes through its owning leaf, not a blanket wait for unrelated #2892 work |
| Production typed collaboration, scoped resources, durable decisions/exact approvals/effects, budgets and recovery | Open #2912 under #2892; #2913 is bounded research only | M6 is natively blocked by #2912 in addition to M5; M7 consumes its production evidence through M6 |
| Source revision extraction | #3790 under #3519 | Independent of outstanding collaboration work; M4/M5 final amended-model acceptance depends on the new source/publication path |
| Prepared publication material retention | #2892 owning Runtime foundation; [concrete prerequisite request](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/2892#issuecomment-6641948798) | T066 cannot freeze/deliver until exact reviewed native/model/template material survives GC/restart under non-runnable retention. Existing Published/TestRun scopes and callback leases do not supply that meaning. Source/Core/API/Studio preparation can continue independently; do not duplicate Runtime infrastructure or reorder ETL ownership. |

Source refactoring does not require inventing a second execution model. Do not reparent #2912, reorder #2892's implementation lane, or count research closure as production completion.

## Delivery sequence and exit gates

| Milestone | Work and designs | Required exit evidence |
|---|---|---|
| M0 — Establishment and research | Establish issue hierarchy/goal/owner amendment; inventory current source, Elsa 3 historical leads and #2913; pin .NET Agent Framework packages/source; run structured-output, tool, session, cancellation and recovery probes; inspect Foundry authoring patterns and framework/license/composition limits | Source/version matrix and reproducible executable probes; explicit pass/fail/unsupported results and recommendation. Documentation review alone is not an integration spike |
| M1 — Product and architecture design | PRD; Studio journeys/wireframes; specialist and team vocabulary; authoring/runtime/artifact model; connection/capability matrix; exact publication/versioning; conversation concurrency/retention; tool/knowledge authority; persistence/recovery/approval/budget state transitions; provider adapter boundary; threat/failure analysis | Reviewed ADR/design packet, finite acceptance matrix, implementation specs/tasks and concrete provider/hosting selection. No unproved public-contract freeze |
| M2 — Catalog and publishing | Tenant-scoped draft CRUD, validation, optimistic concurrency, immutable versions, publish/archive/copy, input/output schemas, permissions; activity-provider discovery, artifact compilation and exact-version resolution | Public APIs and persistence integration; published Copywriter discoverable; already-published workflow bindings remain exact within the supported deployment; denied/stale/cross-tenant/deleted-resource controls; within-deployment recovery and clean initialization evidence |
| M3 — Specialist execution | Agent Framework adapter, model/connection capabilities, schema validation, streaming/run evidence, budgets, cancellation, accepted-result durability, fresh/explicit-session execution; supported provider protocols | Same executable invoked from playground/API; deterministic and real pinned-framework protocol tests; restart/cancel/duplicate/timeout/refusal/invalid-output controls. Live model smoke recorded separately |
| M4 — Native and BPMN integration | Named agent activities with generated ports; Sequence/Flowchart and BPMN task bindings; suspend/resume and parent continuation; bounded editorial loop/human task; persisted inputs/output routing | Copywriter → Proofreader → revision/approval runs on both surfaces; saves/reloads; exact artifact refs; restart and approval recovery; no lost/duplicate logical completion or changed BPMN semantics |
| M5 — Studio authoring and evaluations | Agents list/editor, capability-aware connection/model selection, schema/instructions editing, playground, publish/history/copy/archive; saved test cases and evaluation comparison; run timeline linking to parent process | Real browser CRUD/test/publish/use/inspect journeys; permissions, source-owned/read-only versions, validation, persistence, undo/redo where editing applies, cancellation, responsive/accessibility checks; playground and process share runtime path |
| M6 — Tools, knowledge and bounded teams | Authorized function/workflow tools and MCP adapter; explicit versioned knowledge/context bindings; durable exact approvals and effect identities; pattern-based team configuration and activity publication using MAF where proved; coordinate #2912 production obligations | Read-only and approved mutating tool witnesses, denied access, scoped knowledge, bounded writer/reviewer and concurrent team journeys, barriers/visibility/budget/restart/late-result controls; no silent external-effect replay |
| M7 — Integrated qualification and delivery | Supported provider/host/store matrix; packaged consumer witness; declared pre-GA reset/recreation/republish and within-deployment recovery; operational/user/module-author docs and samples; complete editorial/native/BPMN/team acceptance; exact-head review/CI and resulting-main verification | Every acceptance row has observed evidence or an explicitly owner-accepted scope decision. Required checks pass on reviewed head; descendant main verified; hierarchy/goal closed only after product delivery |

M0–M3 retain their baseline ordering and historical receipts. The merged T064–T071 amendment above governs the next source/publication work before amended-model contract freeze. M0 precedes M1 decisions. M1 precedes production contract freeze. M2 and the required M3 mechanisms precede M4. M5 can produce prototypes during M1 but production UI consumes reviewed M2/M3 contracts. M6 follows the specialist lifecycle and respects #2912's owning lane. M7 closes all milestones. One active implementation leaf; independent review lanes are allowed. Elaborate each next implementation leaf when its prerequisites are concrete; keep later checklists in these epics until then.

## Research spikes

Each spike records an exact source/package version, a question, bounded runnable experiment, expected/observed results, limitations and an adopt/revise/reject recommendation.

1. **Repository/history baseline:** confirm current Agent/Weaver, activity providers, artifact publication, connections/secrets, runtime work/checkpoint, Studio and BPMN contracts; inspect #2913's actual findings. Elsa 3 user-described personas are a product requirement unless independently verified source is available. Do not access organization-off-limits legacy extension repositories.
2. **Agent Framework execution:** real pinned .NET SDK with deterministic IChatClient fixture; dynamic JSON schema, plain-text result, function tool, cancellation, streaming/usage/refusal/invalid output, multiple model connections; optional authorized live-model smoke.
3. **Continuity and recovery:** serialize/restore supported session state, fresh isolation, concurrent same-session access, version change, restart before/after model result/tool dispatch/approval. Specify ambiguous outcomes and single ownership.
4. **Publication/composition:** smallest agent-defined activity through the real provider/compiler/runtime and BPMN binding; input/output schema, exact agent ref and no Design dependency at runtime. Prove externally packaged contribution before widening public APIs.
5. **Team feasibility:** compare Elsa-native explicit composition with bounded MAF team orchestration; pinpoint state/checkpoint/retry/cancel authority, barrier behavior and session/memory visibility. Reuse #2913 and #2912 rather than declaring a new execution model.
6. **Foundry and Studio:** compare author/test/evaluate/publish/inspect journeys; produce low-clutter Elsa-native wireframes and the capability/settings matrix. Distinguish inspiration from actual interoperability.

## Finite product acceptance matrix

- [ ] A1: Tenant-authorized Agent source CRUD, one typed public contract and model settings through shared Workflow/Agent working-copy CAS/snapshot/history mechanics; unpublished source discovery and read-only generated activities/configuration source.
- [ ] A2: Playground uses the production runtime and records exact draft snapshot or published version, connection/model identity, inputs, output, usage and errors without credentials/private reasoning.
- [ ] A3: Exact source snapshots publish through shared provider/preflight/reservation/receipt coordination into discoverable read-only activities with usable ports; release/index repair is receipt-authoritative, and explicit upgrade/copy/retirement preserves bindings within the supported deployment.
